newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Frontier says faces Vietnam well gas delay.
newsitem.headline: Frontier says faces Vietnam well gas delay.

text.p: Operations to determine if a natural gas find in the onshore Hanoi Basin of Vietnam were commercial have been delayed due to a technical problem, Frontier Petroleum NL said on Wednesday.
An attempt to fracture the D14-3 well on May 16 was abandoned after problems, possibly associated with bacterially degraded chemicals, caused the test to plug up, Frontier said.
Replacement chemicals are being airfreighted to Vietnam to replace the existing chemicals, Frontier said.
Pre-fracture injection testing of the D14-3 well had previously indicated no obstructions, Frontier said.
Replacement chemicals are expected to arrive on the site by May 23, when fracture treating will restart, it said.

The fracturing operations are designed to determine if commercial flow rates can be achieved which would enable gas contract negotiations to be concluded to supply the Tien Hai power station, the company has said.
The D14-3 well was shut in on April 30 after flowing gas at a stabilised rate of 180,000 cubic feet per day, Anzoil said.
D14-3, the second appraisal well on the Song Tra Ly D14 gas field, was drilled to a final total depth of 4,903 metres.
D14-3 encountered gas in 38 metres of net sand in Zones One, Two and Three as compared to 49 metres in the D14-1x discovery well and 43 metres in the D14-2 appraisal well.

Frontier holds a minority interest in the Production Sharing Contract (PSC) for the onshore Hanoi Basin. Anzoil NL, thorugh its wholly-owned subsidiary Anzoil (Asia) Pte Ltd, holds the majority and is operator.
Their stakes were originally 80/20 but they are now in dispute over their respective holdings since Frontier failed to meet a drawdown notice in February.

Anzoil won the first round of a legal battle over the Anzoil (Asia) shareholders' agreement when the Western Australian Supreme Court affirmed Anzoil's interpretation of one factor in the agreement's dilution formula for default.

Both companies appeared on May 16 before the Western Australian Supreme Court, which is expected to determine shortly what the total dilution will be, Frontier chief executive David Hayes told Reuters on Wednesday.
Anzoil said recently its additional equity in Anzoil (Asia) is likely to be at least 4.4672 percent.

Hayes said a final interest held by Frontier of between 16 and 20 percent may weigh heavily on the company, particularly as it attempts to locate resource assets independent of Anzoil that are already in production.
"Maybe a 10 percent interest would be more manageable for a company the size of Frontier" Hayes said.
Hayes said Frontier was also open to a farm-in arrangement where Frontier would be carried by another party.
